title: Plant Health & IPM
learningOutcome: Diagnose plant-health problems from evidence, build scouting and sanitation systems, distinguish major cannabis pests and diseases, manage HLVd risk, combine compatible IPM tactics and verify whether interventions actually reduce pressure.
evidenceBoundary: Plant symptoms often overlap. This curriculum does not treat a photograph, color pattern, pest count or single environmental reading as a universal diagnosis or action threshold. Confirmation, crop context and local legal product restrictions remain part of responsible plant-health management.

chapters.title: IPM Thinking, Scouting & Thresholds
chapters.objective: Build a repeatable scouting system that separates observation, identification, risk assessment and action instead of treating every symptom as a spray decision.

lessons.title: IPM starts before a pest or disease is visible
lessons.summary: Integrated pest management combines prevention, exclusion, sanitation, monitoring, identification and multiple control tactics. The goal is to reduce establishment and spread while preserving crop health and useful biological controls.
lessons.cultivation: Design the crop so inspection, sanitation and response are possible before pressure becomes severe.
lessons.observe: Record scouting dates, zones, crop stage, pest or symptom counts, environmental context and actions taken.

lessons.title: A symptom is evidence, not a diagnosis
lessons.summary: Leaf spots, chlorosis, wilting, root browning and distorted growth can arise from pests, pathogens, root stress, water chemistry or environmental injury. Diagnosis improves when symptom pattern is paired with direct evidence.
lessons.cultivation: Do not choose a treatment from color or one photograph alone; first look for organisms, structures, distribution and recent environmental changes.
lessons.observe: Map affected plant parts, undersides, roots, stems, neighboring plants and progression over time.

lessons.title: Scouting must include representative hidden surfaces
lessons.summary: Many important pests begin on leaf undersides, meristems, stems, media surfaces or protected flower sites, so top-down visual inspection can miss early pressure.
lessons.cultivation: Use a fixed route and inspect the same plant zones plus rotating random plants so trends can be compared over time.
lessons.observe: Record plants inspected, leaves per plant, canopy layer, traps checked and inaccessible zones.

lessons.title: Action thresholds are crop-specific decision rules
lessons.summary: A useful threshold considers pest identity, crop stage, rate of increase, biological-control presence, damage risk and regulatory constraints. A universal count is rarely transferable across systems.
lessons.cultivation: Define local escalation rules from trend and crop risk rather than copying one number from another facility.
lessons.observe: Track counts per sampling unit and direction of change before and after each intervention.

chapters.title: Exclusion, Sanitation & Clean Stock
chapters.objective: Prevent organisms from entering or moving through the crop and protect propagation material from becoming a silent distribution system.

lessons.title: Clean stock has disproportionate value
lessons.summary: Mother plants and propagation material can distribute pathogens or pests to many downstream plants. Some infections may be mild or visually subtle in stock plants while still reducing rooting and later performance.
lessons.cultivation: Treat mother-stock health as a separate quality-control system with inspection and testing appropriate to the pathogen risk.
lessons.observe: Record source, clone batch, stock-plant symptoms, rooting performance and test results where used.

lessons.title: Sanitation works by breaking transmission opportunities
lessons.summary: Tools, hands, benches, containers, water splash and plant debris can move inoculum or contaminated sap. Sanitation is strongest when the contact pathway is known and the procedure is repeatable.
lessons.cultivation: Separate clean and dirty work, remove debris promptly and use validated cleaning procedures for the target organism and surface.
lessons.observe: Document what was cleaned, method or contact time where applicable, worker flow and recurring contamination points.

lessons.title: Quarantine protects the established crop
lessons.summary: New genetics, returned plants or suspect material should not immediately share airflow, tools or handling pathways with established clean stock.
lessons.cultivation: Create an intake period that allows visual inspection, pest checks and testing when warranted before integration.
lessons.observe: Record origin, intake date, isolation location, observations and release criteria.

lessons.title: Water and propagation systems can connect plants biologically
lessons.summary: Shared irrigation, runoff, recirculating water and wet propagation surfaces can create common pathways for root pathogens or other microbes.
lessons.cultivation: Map shared water and drainage connections when investigating repeated root disease rather than treating each pot as independent.
lessons.observe: Record irrigation source, recirculation, drainage contact, root symptoms and spatial clustering.

chapters.title: Arthropod Pests & Damage Identification
chapters.objective: Recognize major piercing-sucking and mite pests by direct evidence, characteristic damage and location while avoiding look-alike diagnoses.

lessons.title: Spider mites combine feeding injury with visible colonies
lessons.summary: Twospotted spider mites feed on leaves and can produce stippling, bronzing, webbing and clustered colonies as populations rise; early infestations may be localized.
lessons.cultivation: Confirm mites or eggs with magnification before assuming every stippled leaf is a mite problem.
lessons.observe: Inspect leaf undersides and record live mites, eggs, webbing, damaged area and affected canopy zones.

lessons.title: Russet and broad mites demand magnification
lessons.summary: Hemp russet mites and broad mites are much smaller than common spider mites and can cause distorted, bronzed or stunted growth that resembles nutrient or environmental stress.
lessons.cultivation: Escalate to appropriate magnification when new growth distorts without obvious insects or when damage persists after abiotic causes are checked.
lessons.observe: Sample symptomatic meristems or leaves and document magnification method, organism counts and plant distribution.

lessons.title: Cannabis aphids reveal themselves through insects and cast skins
lessons.summary: Aphids cluster on tender tissues and leaf undersides, remove phloem sap and may leave honeydew or cast skins that are stronger evidence than plant response alone.
lessons.cultivation: Base control decisions on confirmed colonies and trend rather than leaf curl alone.
lessons.observe: Count aphids on defined shoots or leaves and note winged forms, natural enemies and colony expansion.

lessons.title: Damage severity depends on timing and population pressure
lessons.summary: Piercing-sucking pests can reduce vigor and alter physiology, but outcome depends on density, duration, plant stage and environmental conditions.
lessons.cultivation: Use repeated counts and plant-performance records to decide whether pressure is rising, stable or being suppressed.
lessons.observe: Pair pest counts with new-growth rate, leaf damage, canopy distribution and biological-control activity.

chapters.title: Powdery Mildew, Botrytis & Root Disease
chapters.objective: Connect disease symptoms with pathogen biology, susceptible tissue, moisture conditions and confirmation methods before selecting management tactics.

lessons.title: Powdery mildew is a surface-visible disease with crop-wide epidemiology
lessons.summary: White powdery colonies on leaves can be conspicuous, but the management problem includes infected stock, spore movement, canopy conditions and missed early lesions.
lessons.cultivation: Do not treat visible powder on one leaf as the entire problem; inspect connected plants and environmental conditions.
lessons.observe: Record lesion location, affected plants, new lesions over time, canopy density and environmental history.

lessons.title: Botrytis risk increases inside dense, moist flowers
lessons.summary: Botrytis can colonize wounded or senescing tissue and dense inflorescences where local humidity and poor air exchange differ from room averages.
lessons.cultivation: Inspect interior flower tissue and address moisture management, sanitation and plant density rather than relying only on room RH.
lessons.observe: Record flower location, internal discoloration or softening, condensation evidence, local airflow and spread.

lessons.title: Root browning has infectious and noninfectious causes
lessons.summary: Fusarium and Pythium can cause root disease, but waterlogging, oxygen limitation and physical root decline can also brown roots. Accurate diagnosis requires more than color.
lessons.cultivation: Check root-zone conditions and pathogen evidence together before assigning a disease label.
lessons.observe: Document root color, texture and odor, irrigation frequency, media saturation, temperature and affected-plant pattern.

lessons.title: Disease management targets survival, spread and susceptibility
lessons.summary: Integrated disease management combines sanitation, clean propagation, environment, tolerant genetics where available, biological tools and other validated controls.
lessons.cultivation: Choose compatible tactics that act on different parts of the disease cycle rather than depending on one rescue product.
lessons.observe: Track which tactic targets host, pathogen or environment and whether incidence changes afterward.

chapters.title: HLVd & Systemic Pathogen Management
chapters.objective: Understand why asymptomatic systemic infection requires testing, clean-stock discipline and transmission control rather than symptom-only scouting.

lessons.title: HLVd can be present before obvious symptoms
lessons.summary: Hop latent viroid can persist in cannabis with limited or inconsistent visible symptoms, especially in stock material, while affecting rooting, vigor, flower development and chemistry downstream.
lessons.cultivation: Do not use visual appearance alone to certify high-value mother stock as clean when HLVd risk is material.
lessons.observe: Record lineage, source, performance drift, suspect symptoms and laboratory test results where available.

lessons.title: Mechanical transmission makes workflow design important
lessons.summary: Contaminated sap on tools or hands can move viroid between plants; propagation and repeated pruning create many contact events.
lessons.cultivation: Sequence work from clean to suspect areas and apply validated tool sanitation according to the production risk plan.
lessons.observe: Map high-contact operations and record sanitation compliance and shared-tool events.

lessons.title: Testing quality depends on sampling quality
lessons.summary: A laboratory method cannot correct for a poor or unrepresentative sample. Tissue choice, plant stage, labeling and chain of identity determine whether results can support decisions.
lessons.cultivation: Use a defined sampling protocol and preserve identity from plant to result.
lessons.observe: Record plant ID, tissue sampled, date, sampler, assay or lab and result; investigate conflicts with crop performance.

lessons.title: Containment decisions should consider network exposure
lessons.summary: When a systemic pathogen is detected, the relevant unit may include connected clones, shared mother stock and tools rather than only the positive plant.
lessons.cultivation: Trace propagation and contact relationships before declaring the incident isolated.
lessons.observe: Document mother-to-clone relationships, shared tools or areas and dates so exposed material can be prioritized.

chapters.title: Biological, Cultural & Product-Based Controls
chapters.objective: Compare control tactics by target, timing, compatibility and evidence while avoiding the idea that one product replaces prevention and diagnosis.

lessons.title: Biological control is a population-management strategy
lessons.summary: Predators, parasitoids and microbial agents work through living interactions that depend on release timing, prey density, environment and compatibility with other inputs.
lessons.cultivation: Plan biological controls from the target pest and crop environment, not from a generic beneficial-insect list.
lessons.observe: Record organism released, rate or location, environmental conditions, pest trend and observed establishment.

lessons.title: Cultural control changes the system that favors the problem
lessons.summary: Canopy density, irrigation, sanitation, infected stock, crop residue and worker movement can make pests or diseases easier or harder to establish.
lessons.cultivation: Correct repeatable system drivers alongside direct suppression so pressure does not immediately rebuild.
lessons.observe: Track the suspected driver and verify whether changing it alters incidence or population trend.

lessons.title: Product efficacy is conditional
lessons.summary: A legally permitted product may perform differently with coverage, life stage, environment, resistance status and timing; cannabis pesticide rules also vary by jurisdiction.
lessons.cultivation: Use only legally permitted products and follow the label; verify control with post-treatment scouting rather than assuming application equals success.
lessons.observe: Record product, legal label context, target, application date and pre/post counts without publishing unsafe mixing advice.

lessons.title: Compatibility matters in an IPM program
lessons.summary: Some interventions can disrupt beneficial organisms, plant tissues or later diagnostic interpretation, so tactics should be sequenced intentionally.
lessons.cultivation: Review how each intervention affects biological controls, crop stage and diagnostic evidence before stacking treatments.
lessons.observe: Maintain an intervention timeline and note non-target effects, pest rebound or beneficial-population changes.

chapters.title: Environment, Canopy & Disease Pressure
chapters.objective: Use plant microclimate and root-zone measurements to explain changing disease risk instead of treating pathogens as independent of cultivation conditions.

lessons.title: Canopy microclimate can diverge from room sensors
lessons.summary: Dense leaves and flowers create local humidity, temperature and airflow conditions that may favor disease even when the room average appears acceptable.
lessons.cultivation: Measure or inspect representative interior canopy zones when disease repeatedly appears in dense areas.
lessons.observe: Compare room and canopy temperature or RH, condensation evidence, density and airflow.

lessons.title: Irrigation decisions influence root-disease risk
lessons.summary: Repeated saturation, poor drainage and warm root zones can weaken roots and create conditions that complicate pathogen management.
lessons.cultivation: Treat irrigation pattern and media physical condition as part of root-disease investigation.
lessons.observe: Record substrate water status, dryback trend, root-zone temperature, drainage and irrigation events before diagnosis.

lessons.title: Plant stress can change susceptibility and symptom expression
lessons.summary: Heat, water stress, root damage, nutrient imbalance and wounding can alter plant defenses or create entry points while also producing symptoms that resemble infection.
lessons.cultivation: Stabilize major abiotic stressors while collecting pathogen evidence so the diagnostic picture is not confounded.
lessons.observe: Record recent environmental excursions, training or wounds, root events and timing relative to symptoms.

lessons.title: Canopy design affects both risk and detectability
lessons.summary: Very dense canopies can retain moisture and also prevent workers from inspecting stems, leaf undersides and flower interiors.
lessons.cultivation: Treat inspection access and air distribution as plant-health design criteria, not just labor considerations.
lessons.observe: Document inaccessible zones, scouting time, airflow symptoms and disease clustering by canopy position.

chapters.title: Verification, Records & Escalation
chapters.objective: Turn IPM into a learning system by preserving evidence, verifying outcomes and escalating uncertain or high-risk cases to appropriate diagnostics.

lessons.title: Every intervention should have an outcome measure
lessons.summary: Without a pre-treatment baseline and post-treatment observation, the crop cannot show whether the action actually changed the problem.
lessons.cultivation: Define what success will look like before acting, such as declining counts, no new lesions or improved new growth.
lessons.observe: Record baseline, action, follow-up dates and the same measurement unit each time.

lessons.title: Image records are strongest when standardized
lessons.summary: Photos become more useful when scale, lighting, viewpoint, plant ID and tissue location are consistent rather than dramatic but incomparable.
lessons.cultivation: Capture overview and close-up images with a reference scale and repeat the same angles during follow-up.
lessons.observe: Store plant ID, date, tissue site, lighting or magnification and whether the image is observation or interpretation.

lessons.title: Escalate when the cost of being wrong is high
lessons.summary: Systemic pathogens, rapidly spreading disease, unknown organisms, repeated control failure or production-wide symptoms justify laboratory or specialist confirmation.
lessons.cultivation: Use external diagnostics when visual evidence cannot reliably distinguish high-consequence alternatives.
lessons.observe: Record the question being tested, sample origin and how the result changes management.

lessons.title: Records reveal recurring system failures
lessons.summary: Repeated maps of pest pressure, disease incidence and environmental excursions can expose source areas, seasonal patterns or process failures invisible in one event.
lessons.cultivation: Review IPM data periodically for recurrence by room, cultivar, worker flow, stock source and crop stage.
lessons.observe: Summarize incidence, counts, interventions, response time and recurrence instead of keeping only narrative notes.
